name: Colin Varga

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to any company, union, party or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I drive tractors on Ashby Grange, about nine hundred hectares of wheat, barley and oilseed rape, for a family that also rents out half the land to a bigger outfit. This time of year I'm rolling fields after drilling, hauling grain out of the store, and cleaning out the dryer. Most days are eight to six, but in harvest it's sunrise to whenever the dew comes down.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the big days, honestly. Combining in August with the radio on and the trailers going back and forth, you feel like part of something. What wears me out is that I'm the one who gets the boring jobs. Rob, the foreman, does the spraying and the drilling because he's got the qualifications, and I get the roller and the brush.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How much of the tractor work is already done by computer?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: More than people think. The big tractor has GPS autosteer, so it drives itself in straight lines down the field and I just turn it at the ends. I was suspicious of it at first, but after the first season it was obviously better than me. My lines used to wander like a drunk snake.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the first picture. Picture this. AI stays a handy tool, like a better search engine. Hiring, pay and prices carry on the way they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's useful in small ways. I already ask a chatbot now and then, like when the sprayer threw an error code and Rob wasn't answering his phone. It told me it was a blocked nozzle filter and it was right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, if nothing changes, my problem is still pay. I'm on the bottom rate, my girlfriend Neha's a teaching assistant, and between us we've got about three weeks of money if the car went. That's not an AI problem, that's just farming wages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep pushing to get my spraying certificate, so I'm not stuck on the roller. That's the main thing. It's a few days' course and an exam, and the farm said they'd pay for it 'next year' for two years now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine, mostly. A bit stuck, but it's my own kind of stuck.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why do you think the farm keeps putting off paying for the certificate?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because Rob does the spraying and there's no point having two of us, from their side. It's money spent on me that only pays off if Rob leaves or gets ill. I get it, I just don't like it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything you'd change about the job, if this picture held?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A proper pay scale. Like teachers have, so you know if you do the certificate you go up a step. Neha knows exactly what she'll earn in three years. I've no idea what I'll earn next month if the price of wheat drops.

S0.say: I'd say it's useful in small ways, like when a chatbot correctly told me a sprayer error was a blocked nozzle filter. It's a tool, not a big deal.
S0.think: If nothing changes my real problem is still pay, not AI. Neha and I have about three weeks of money between us, and that's just farming wages.
S0.do: Keeps pushing the farm to pay for his spraying certificate, a few days' course and an exam. Keeps doing the rolling and grain hauling meanwhile.
S0.feel: Mostly fine, a bit stuck. It's a familiar kind of frustration.
S0.quote: Neha knows exactly what she'll earn in three years. I've no idea what I'll earn next month if the price of wheat drops.
S0.fieldNote: He's already using AI tools in a practical, occasional way and talks about them without fuss. The pay scale idea came from comparing himself to his girlfriend's job. The certificate has been promised 'next year' twice, which says a lot about where he stands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Thanks. Now picture this. Very capable AI exists, but it spreads slowly, over ten years or more. Some tasks disappear, but few whole jobs do. Companies hire fewer beginners. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's what's been happening in farming for fifty years anyway. There used to be eight men on this farm, now there's three of us. Fewer beginners is just the same story with a new name.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I scraped in just before the door shut. If they'd had another season of the autosteer working well and a better drill, would they have taken me on? Probably not. So I've got to make myself worth more than a roller driver before the next round.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Get the spraying ticket, even if I pay half myself. Maybe start asking Rob to let me run the yield maps on the computer after harvest, the colour maps that show which bits of field did well. Nobody else wants to look at them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit uneasy, but I can see what to do, which helps.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd pay half the course yourself. Where would that money come from?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd skip a holiday. Neha wants to go to the coast for a week in summer and I'd have to say not this year. That's a conversation I'm not looking forward to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who do you think benefits when farms need fewer workers?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Landowners and the big machinery firms. The yield goes up, the wage bill goes down, and the money goes to whoever owns the land and the kit. I'd want some of it to come back to the village, a bus that runs more than twice a day, a doctor that's open. That's where the money went out of.

S1.say: I'd say this has been happening in farming for fifty years. My farm went from eight workers to three, so fewer beginners is the same story with a new name.
S1.think: I think I scraped in just before the door shut. I need to make myself worth more than a roller driver before the next round of cutbacks.
S1.do: Gets the spraying certificate, paying half himself if needed by skipping a summer holiday. Asks the foreman to let him run the yield maps on the farm computer after harvest.
S1.feel: Uneasy, but he can see what to do, and that steadies him.
S1.quote: There used to be eight men on this farm, now there's three of us. Fewer beginners is just the same story with a new name.
S1.fieldNote: He frames slow AI as a continuation of farm history, which makes it less frightening to him. He picked the yield maps because nobody else wants them, a smart and modest move. His politics surfaced as local services, not slogans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Thank you. Next one. Within 5 years, AI assistants that can act on their own handle most routine office work. There are layoffs and pay pressure in office jobs. Some new AI-related jobs appear, and politicians argue loudly about what to do. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's not just an office thing, it'll hit the farm office too. Ashby's got a woman, Gill, who does the payroll, the grain contracts and all the forms for the subsidy. If an AI can do that, she's gone, and she's been there twenty years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me personally, it doesn't change much. A computer can fill in forms, it can't haul grain. But I'd be lying if I said I hadn't thought that maybe I could do some of Gill's bits with the AI. I don't like that I thought that. It would be a step up for me and a step out the door for her.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably learn whatever system they bring in, if it's proven. I'd want to see it working for a season first. And I'd go to the union meeting. There's a farm workers' branch in the market town that meets in the pub once a month and I've never gone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy for Gill. A bit hopeful for me, and a bit ashamed of the hopeful bit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd take some of Gill's work. What would you say to her?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want to say it to her face before anyone else did. Something like, I'm not after your job, they asked me to. But she'd know. You can't really say that nicely.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want politicians to argue for, out of all the noise?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That the money saved goes somewhere. If a company saves Gill's wage, some of that should go into training and a decent payment while people find something else. Not just a speech.

S2.say: I'd say it isn't just an office thing, because the farm office will be hit too. Gill does our payroll, grain contracts and subsidy forms, and she's been there twenty years.
S2.think: For me it doesn't change much, because a computer can't haul grain. But part of me thinks I could take over some of Gill's work with AI, and I don't like that I thought that.
S2.do: Learns any new office system once it has been proven for a season. Starts going to the monthly farm workers' union meeting in the market town.
S2.feel: Uneasy for Gill, quietly hopeful for himself, and ashamed of the hope.
S2.quote: I'd be lying if I said I hadn't thought that maybe I could do some of Gill's bits with the AI. I don't like that I thought that.
S2.fieldNote: An honest admission of ambition at a colleague's expense, which he immediately judged. His steady style showed in wanting a full season of proof before trusting a new system. The union meeting he's never attended came up as a concrete first step.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now a faster version. Within 2 to 3 years, AI matches skilled professionals at most thinking work. Lots of office and professional workers lose their jobs. Share and house prices boom. There's a political crisis over who should get the gains. Physical jobs are mostly untouched. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the people who own the land and the shares are going to do very well out of this, and the rest of us are watching. I'd be posting about it, probably. Tax the gains, put it into people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: What I really think is it doesn't touch my job, but it touches everything around it. If Neha's school loses office staff, she ends up doing their work too. And if house prices boom, we're never buying anything. We rent above the hairdresser in the village, and the landlord will put the rent up the first chance he gets.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay put at Ashby, because a physical job is the safe place in this one. Keep my head down, do the certificate, maybe pick up weekend work hauling for a contractor. I'd push Neha to join her union too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but not about myself. About rent, and about everyone else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to grain prices in this picture, do you think?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I don't know. People still eat bread. But the landowner's land would be worth a fortune, so maybe they sell up to someone rich who wants a country house. That's what scares me more than robots, a new owner who doesn't farm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd keep your head down and also post about taxing the gains. Would your boss see those posts?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably, he's on the same village group. I'd keep it general. Tax the big companies. I wouldn't name landowners, because my landowner signs my wages.

S3.say: I'd say the people who own land and shares will do very well while the rest of us watch. I'd post that the gains should be taxed and put back into people.
S3.think: It doesn't touch my job, but it touches everything around it. Neha would end up covering for lost office staff at her school, and rising house prices mean we'd never buy and our rent would go up.
S3.do: Stays at Ashby Grange, finishes the spraying certificate and picks up weekend haulage work for a contractor. Encourages Neha to join her union and keeps his online posts general so he doesn't name his own employer.
S3.feel: Anxious, but more about rent and other people than about his own job.
S3.quote: That's what scares me more than robots, a new owner who doesn't farm.
S3.fieldNote: He spotted a risk the card doesn't mention: soaring land values tempting the owners to sell to someone who won't farm. He's careful about speaking out, softening his posts because the landowner pays him. Rent above the hairdresser is a real, close worry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Thanks for staying with me. Last one. Everything in the previous picture happens, and on top of that, general-purpose robots arrive in warehouses, kitchens, building sites, farms and care homes within 3 to 5 years. Hands-on work is no longer a safe place to be. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's the big one. Fields are the easiest place in the world for a robot, flat, open, no customers. If they're putting robots in kitchens, they're definitely putting them in wheat fields.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'm the first to go. Rob's got the knowledge and the certificates. I'm the one who turns the tractor at the end of the field, and the autosteer already does the rest. A driverless tractor doesn't need turning, does it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want to watch one working before I believed it, like the autosteer. Then I'd ask to be the person who looks after them, refills them, fixes the small stuff, because someone's got to drive to the field when one gets stuck in a wet corner. And I'd ask the union what they're doing, loudly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. My stomach drops when I picture the yard with no tractors in it, just a charging shed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Neha that evening, after you found out the farm was buying them?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got about three weeks, so don't panic but don't book anything. Then I'd probably go quiet and watch telly and not say much else. That's what my dad did when the quarry shut.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Your dad went through a closure. What did you learn from that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That you don't wait to be told. He waited for them to say it out loud, and by then all the other jobs nearby had gone to the men who moved first. If I saw a robot in a field near us, I'd be asking questions that week, not the next season.

S4.say: I'd say this is the big one, because flat, open fields are the easiest place for a robot. If robots are going into kitchens, they're definitely going into wheat fields.
S4.think: I'm the first to go, because the foreman has the knowledge and I'm the one who turns the tractor at the end of the field. A driverless tractor doesn't need turning.
S4.do: Watches a driverless tractor working before believing in it, then asks to be the person who looks after, refuels and fixes the machines. Pushes the union for answers and starts asking about jobs the same week robots appear nearby.
S4.feel: Alarmed, with a drop in his stomach at the picture of a yard with only a charging shed.
S4.quote: I'm the one who turns the tractor at the end of the field, and the autosteer already does the rest. A driverless tractor doesn't need turning, does it.
S4.fieldNote: His steady habit of wanting proof stayed, but his father's quarry closure pushed him to move early. He sees his own role precisely, as the gap the autosteer leaves. Quiet at home, active at work, which mirrors his father in a way he noticed himself.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The robots one, because my job is exactly the bit that's left over once the autosteer's done its work. What would help is training that's paid, so I'm not choosing between rent and learning. And some rule that if a farm buys robots, part of the saving goes to the workers it lets go.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe what happens to villages. Every job that goes off a farm is a family that stops shopping in the village. Our pub nearly shut last year. You can't put a robot in the darts team.

headlineQuote: I'm the one who turns the tractor at the end of the field, and the autosteer already does the rest. A driverless tractor doesn't need turning, does it.
portrait: Colin Varga is a 27-year-old tractor driver on a 900-hectare grain and oilseed farm, renting a flat above the village hairdresser with his girlfriend Neha, a teaching assistant. He uses AI tools now and then and accepts new machinery once he has seen it work, as he did with GPS autosteer. Through the office scenarios he worries more about colleagues, rent and his village than his own job. The robot scenario hits him hardest, because he sees his role as the small gap the autosteer leaves. Shaped by his father's quarry closure, he would move early, push the union and ask to be the one who looks after the machines.
biggestWorry: The fast robots scenario, because his job is exactly the part of tractor work the autosteer doesn't yet do.
whatWouldHelp: Paid training so he isn't choosing between rent and learning, and a rule that farms buying robots share part of the saving with the workers they let go.
